content: Erythema gyratum repens (EGR) is a rare and highly specific paraneoplastic syndrome that predominantly affects older individuals. It is characterized by distinctive wood-grain-like, scaly skin eruptions accompanied by intense pruritus. The exact cause of EGR remains unknown, but immunologic and toxicologic mechanisms related to an associated tumor are strongly suspected. The condition was first described in 1952 by Dr. John A. Gammel, a dermatologist, in a 55-year-old patient who presented with pruritic, scaly skin eruptions and was later diagnosed with poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the breast with axillary lymph node metastases. Dr. Gammel initially referred to the condition as erythema gyratum migrans but later renamed it erythema gyratum repens to reflect the crawling nature of the skin lesions, which do not migrate but rather expand concentrically in the affected areas. EGR is most commonly associated with internal malignancies, particularly lung or bronchogenic cancer, esophageal cancer, and breast cancer. However, it can also occur in non-neoplastic conditions such as tuberculosis, autoimmune disorders, or CREST syndrome. The skin eruptions are pathognomonic, presenting as wavy, erythematous concentric bands arranged in parallel rings with a fine trailing edge of scales, often described as resembling wood grain. These lesions typically spare the face, hands, and feet but can expand rapidly, up to 1 cm per day. Bullae may also form within the erythematous areas. Histopathological examination of EGR lesions reveals non-specific findings, including acanthosis, focal parakeratosis, spongiosis, and a perivascular mononuclear infiltrate in the superficial dermis. Immunofluorescence studies have demonstrated patterns of IgG, C3, and C4 deposition at the basement membrane, supporting an immunologic mechanism. Proposed theories include tumor-induced antibodies cross-reacting with skin basement membrane antigens, tumor-derived polypeptides rendering skin antigens immunogenic, or deposition of tumor antigen-antibody complexes causing reactive dermatitis. EGR is primarily diagnosed clinically based on its characteristic skin lesions. It is considered a cutaneous marker of malignancy with high specificity, necessitating an urgent and thorough paraneoplastic workup to identify any underlying malignancy. This workup may include imaging studies such as CT or PET scans, endoscopy, tumor marker evaluation, and blood tests to exclude systemic involvement. Treatment of EGR focuses on identifying and managing the underlying malignancy. Surgical resection of the tumor, chemotherapy, or palliative care may be employed depending on the tumor type and stage. Symptomatic treatments, including systemic or topical steroids, vitamin A, and immunosuppressive agents like azathioprine, are generally ineffective in relieving the intense pruritus and skin manifestations. Improvement of EGR and associated symptoms is typically observed following successful treatment of the underlying malignancy. However, recurrence of the skin lesions may occur, particularly in cases of tumor metastasis. The prognosis of EGR depends on the type and stage of the associated malignancy. While some patients experience complete resolution of skin lesions and pruritus after tumor treatment, others may have persistent symptoms or recurrence. In some cases, death may occur within weeks to months of malignancy diagnosis, as seen in Dr. Gammel's original patient. EGR is a rare dermatologic condition, with an average age of onset in the seventh decade of life and a male-to-female ratio of 2:1. It predominantly affects Caucasians and has no established risk factors or screening tests. The majority of patients present with severely pruritic skin lesions several months before the diagnosis of malignancy. Other associated symptoms may include weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, and fever. A history of tobacco smoking or a family history of neoplasm is common among affected individuals. Differentiating EGR from other dermatologic conditions is crucial. Reactive gyrate erythemas, such as erythema annulare centrifugum (EAC) and necrolytic migratory erythema (NME), may mimic EGR but are not always associated with malignancy. Other conditions to consider include erythema marginatum rheumaticum, erythema chronicum migrans, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and neonatal lupus erythematosus. In summary, EGR is a rare but significant paraneoplastic syndrome that serves as a cutaneous marker of internal malignancy. Prompt recognition and management of the underlying tumor are essential for improving patient outcomes.
